analysis.title: US midterm elections: What a Democratic sweep means for the economic outlook
key_insights: Democrats won both chambers in the US midterms. Per the NYT nowcast they are heading for a 250+ seat House majority, the largest since 2008, and a 55-45 Senate majority after gaining eight seats, the strongest since 2012.

The Senate filibuster and presidential veto still limit what Democrats can enact. Fidelity expects Democrats to push healthcare, other social spending and clean energy through reconciliation bills, which need only a simple majority.

Fiscal risks are tilted toward further easing. Upcoming government funding and debt ceiling deadlines give Democrats leverage to negotiate spending concessions, and neither party shows much inclination to cut the elevated deficit despite strong growth.

Government funding expires December 11, during the lame-duck session with Republicans still in control of Congress. Limited agreement on full-year appropriations makes a short-term continuing resolution the most likely outcome, which pushes the next deadline into early 2027 and keeps shutdown risk alive.
The debt ceiling could be reached around Q2 2027 under current spending plans. Extraordinary measures could push the 'X date' toward year-end.

Democratic control of the House opens the door to investigations of the Trump administration, including conflicts of interest, prediction markets and possible impeachment proceedings. Removal would need a two-thirds Senate majority, but the proceedings could consume political bandwidth and create headline risk. A Democratic Senate could also block key appointments, including to the Fed.

Democrats flipped four governorships. Texas, Ohio and Georgia, three of them, account for almost a third of planned US data centre capacity. Governors who campaigned on curbing data centre construction are likely to add moratoria and permit restrictions, plus protections on water supply, energy costs and investment incentives.

Tighter state-level data centre regulation could slow AI infrastructure investment. Fidelity calls this a key risk to its macro outlook and says it could gain traction federally ahead of the 2028 elections.

Trump keeps broad executive control over tariffs, immigration and foreign policy. The administration is preparing Section 301 investigations into industrial overcapacity to replace tariffs struck down under IEEPA, so trade restrictions stay a central tool.

Fidelity sees continued upside risk to oil prices from the Iran war. This is a potential supply shock for the global economy, weighs on inflation in energy-importing Europe and Asia, and keeps a bias toward monetary tightening there.

Taiwan and South Korea are most exposed to US AI investment and regulation because of their roles in the AI supply chain. Semiconductor export controls bear more directly on China, and both policy areas sit mostly within executive control.

Fidelity sees little scope for easing in US-China tensions. Tariffs, technology restrictions and supply-chain diversification have bipartisan support. The upcoming APEC summit could clarify near-term trade talks, but the broader trajectory is unlikely to change.

Base case: US growth slows to trend next year after robust growth in 2026. The backdrop includes a renewed Fed hiking cycle, tightening financial conditions and building geopolitical and inflationary shocks.
The economy's reliance on capex and the AI build-out is shifting from the scale of spending to the returns it can generate.
